blocks.text: DNA is present in the nucleus of every living cell. It is a coded plan, or blueprint, for making proteins, which are vital for life; each specific protein is made by a specific gene, a section of DNA. DNA carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all living organisms. Its double helix stores information in the sequence of its four bases and passes it on efficiently and accurately for protein synthesis.

blocks.alt: Top: five boxes, genome (all the DNA, in the nucleus), chromosome (23 pairs in a human cell), gene (a section of DNA for one protein), DNA (bases on a sugar-phosphate chain) and codon (three bases code for one amino acid). Bottom: DNA -> DNA by replication (DNA polymerase), DNA -> mRNA by transcription (RNA polymerase) in the nucleus, and mRNA -> protein by translation (ribosome and tRNA) in the cytoplasm.
blocks.caption: From the genome to the codon, and the flow of genetic information (original diagram after Figures 27.14 and 27.17).
blocks.long_description: Information is stored in the order of bases in DNA, organised as genes on chromosomes. To make a protein, a gene is transcribed into mRNA, which leaves the nucleus; at the ribosome each codon of three bases is matched by a tRNA carrying one particular amino acid, so the base sequence becomes an amino acid sequence.

blocks.text: Genes are organised into larger units called chromosomes; humans receive 23 pairs from their parents. Nearly every cell carries the full set of 23 pairs, but each type of cell uses only some of its genes: a cell that will become a red blood cell switches on the gene for haemoglobin and keeps the gene for keratin switched off.
The structure and function of DNA

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick showed that DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains. Each chain forms a right-handed helix and the two chains coil round each other to form a double helix. The chains are not identical but complementary, and they run in opposite directions: the 3' end of one faces the 5' end of the other. Each chain has a sugar-phosphate backbone with bases projecting at right angles, held by weak hydrogen bonds to the bases of the other chain. Adenine (A) is always opposite thymine (T), and guanine (G) opposite cytosine (C); there are two hydrogen bonds in an A-T pair and three in a G-C pair.

blocks.alt: Top: a chain of alternating P (phosphate) circles and S (sugar) pentagons, each sugar carrying a base, from the 5' end to the 3' end. Bottom: two vertical backbones with arrows pointing in opposite directions and bars of bases between them: A-T and T-A pairs joined by two dashed hydrogen bonds, C-G and G-C pairs by three.
blocks.caption: A polynucleotide chain and DNA base pairing (original diagram after Figures 27.13 and 27.15).
blocks.long_description: The backbone of each strand is a strong covalent chain of sugars and phosphates. The two strands are held together only by hydrogen bonds between paired bases, A with T and G with C, which are weak enough to separate when DNA is copied. Because the pairing is fixed, each strand carries the information needed to rebuild the other.

blocks.text: Genes are the specific regions of DNA that carry genetic information and instruct the cell to make particular proteins. An important process of DNA is self-replication: during the cell cycle DNA is copied, so that at cell division each new cell receives a complete set of genetic material. In this way genetic information passes from one cell to its daughter cells and to the next generation.

blocks.prompt: How many hydrogen bonds join an A-T pair and a G-C pair?
blocks.explanation: Two between A and T; three between G and C.

items: DNA: two antiparallel polynucleotide chains in a right-handed double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953).
A-T (2 hydrogen bonds), G-C (3 hydrogen bonds).
Genes code for proteins; DNA replicates before cell division.
